source: 'Gifts she now rejects, soon she'll give them...'
'Now she doesn't love you, but soon her heart will burn...'
Come to me again and abate my torment!
Give me what I long for!
Guilda, what song is that?
I have absolutely no idea.
It just sort of came to me. You know?
I guess Aphrodite really is my muse!
What in black hell was that? I asked you to play something that would attract a paying audience!
And that's exactly what we did. Look at all of these admiring fans!
We've attracted quite the crowd, it's true.
You idiots. They're only here because they think you're going to take off your skirts.
What? Why would they think that?
Ah, well, that verse you chose...
It's a little—shall we say—romantic?
Well, of course. That's the only sort of verse worth knowing.
You two are a lost cause. A sunk cost. I'll never see a single coin of my money, will I?
I've had enough. I'm returning to the castle.
Well, there goes our last chance to ever deal in at Irma's table again.
There, there. It's all right. She's a cheat anyhow, and we both knew it.
We'll simply have to find some other way to entertain ourselves in this dreadful place, I suppose.
I can think of a few ways you can entertain each other!
Aye! Take 'er sleeves down!
We'll pay yeh!
Y-you're all vile!
Yeah! Shame on you! Our love is not for sale!
Wait. What?
Nothing, nothing. Rosie, let's get out of here!
She's got a lovely sound.
Mm. First lute I ever bought. I've given it a touch-up and it's like new now.
Thought I'd follow a lark or two.
What's yours made of? Such a fascinating surface.
No name you would recognize. It was made in my homeland.
Where are you from?
Same as you, from the looks of it.
You're mistaken, sir.
Some parts of you seem Danish, to a degree. Your fine clothes mark you a part of the local flock.
My sister and I were born here.
Ah. Then by reputation, you are that one they call Lord Laertes.
I've seen your father. Pale little man. So I must admit, you fascinate me.
You're not the first to be curious. If you must know, my mother was a foreigner.
Of course. Hard to imagine she wouldn't be.
What was it like, living with a father like that?
He wanted—wants—to protect us. Sometimes that protection became unbearable.
Often, as a boy, I would ask him why we looked strange, my sister and I. He always feigned confusion.
And his feigned confusion frightened me. I wondered if he didn't truly see that we were different.
Because... others did.
I've been called every horrid thing under the sun, in whispered breath or behind a lifted palm.
Sometimes, when I wander through town, I'll find a stone skidded against my leg from afar, or hear the jeering of children.
But I am who I am. I refuse to hide.
Oh, yes. I'm well familiar.
We draw quite a crowd, don't we? But where there's numbers, there's strength.
And there's fear.
Look around. Everyone's leaving the bar.
That'll be my doing, I'm afraid.
Well. Those same townsfolk drop coins into my till every night by the dozen to have me pour their beer.
They may be nervous now, but they'll be back tonight. This is the cheapest place they can drink. And then—my bar, my rules.
So much as the smallest smirk or slur is dropped, they're out of my establishment forever. By my own hand.
I cannot promise that the world outside is kind, my lord.
But in here, things are different. At least for now.
If you would ever come to play by the fire a while, you would be in good hands and good company.
Bring your own lute next time. We'll play a ditty or three together.
You have my thanks. I shall consider the offer most intently.
Claudius and Hamlet ran to the chapel. They looked upset. I ought to pay them a visit.
Ah. Ophelia. You're back at last.
I'd heard your ship was returned to port...
And so was yours, it seems.
Ophelia. I've returned.
So soon? Oughtn't you to be in Paris by now?
I was at port in Aalborg when I heard the news. About everything happening back here, that is.
The situation in Elsinore has deteriorated quickly.
Are you all right? No one's harmed you?
I'm safe, for now.
There's work to be done, and I intend to act swiftly.
Good. Then there's work to be done, and I intend to act swiftly.
Father wrote me a letter, you know. He explained everything.
About Hamlet's attempt on his life. I doubt that Hamlet could have acted alone.
And what do you intend to do about it?
Ensure no one can ever threaten my family again.
In the wake of his death, I have to imagine Hamlet acting against Father was not his own doing. Someone spurred him.
I intend to raise arms against this sea of troubles.
I heard about what happened to Father. How Hamlet brutalized him.
But I cannot believe Hamlet acted alone. Someone spurred him.
Even with Hamlet dead, the matter is not handled. And I intend to pursue it to its root.
Father's gone, but we're still here. I'm concerned about your safety in all this.
I heard about the circumstances around Hamlet's death.
I've come back to understand. And to sort through what's left.
That is to say, here, by the fire. I'm not ready to return to Elsinore just yet.
Thank you for coming swiftly. He's gone too far this time, Bernardo. Hamlet, I mean.
Threatening Father's life-- he nearly killed the man.
You were there, were you not? I heard you rendered Hamlet unconscious. Prevented further bloodshed.
I was. I am uncertain what would have transpired had your sister not alerted me to the situation.
That's why this has to end. I need you to help me, old friend.
Will you ensure Hamlet is properly contained and brought to justice?
I don't mean rotting in a cell. I mean gone. For good.
He's gone to England. What would you have me do? Hasn't he been punished sufficiently?
No. I want him dead, no matter whose soil he walks on. I know your family must have some connections.
Laertes, I'm afraid it is not so simple.
For all that Hamlet is not in his right mind as of late, the incident with your father was an accident.
He believed his uncle was behind the curtain in the Queen's bedroom, spying on him.
He never intended your father any direct harm. It was horrific, yes, but not a meditated act.
Surely you cannot mean...
That you intend to let Hamlet walk free as a result?
At this stage, I fear having Hamlet executed would only exacerbate the tension in Elsinore, not improve it.
It appeared to be a regrettable incident, but a one-time incident nonetheless.
You-- you're my best friend. The man whose heart I believed in most ardently.
How can you stand here and defend my father's attacker?
You understand the great love I bear for you and your family, Laertes. Always have. Always will.
I am the Captain of the Guard. It is not my place to mete out punishment and retribution and righteous judgement.
It is my place to keep as many people alive as I possibly can, and to maintain the sanctity of the state of Denmark.
You're a man of God. Isn't it said in Matthew, 'An eye for an eye, and tooth for tooth'?
Of course. But that is only the first line of that passage.
'...But I say unto you, that ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.'
It continues, 'Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you.'
I will not stand here and let Hamlet threaten all I hold dear.
If you won't stop him, rest assured that if he ever sets foot on Danish soil again, I will. Farewell.
If you won't stop him, rest assured, I will. Farewell.
You summoned me, my lord?
Ah. Polonius. Come in.
So. Laertes is staying in Elsinore indefinitely, at least for the time being.
What are your thoughts on the matter?
At first I was concerned, but now I find something rather timely in it.
Well. The mood has certainly shifted in the castle suddenly, don't you think?
So much has happened in such a short time.
Mmm. I see.
Polonius, do you often play chess?
I must admit, I haven't quite kept my tactician's instincts sharp! Fancy a match?
Of course, of course. I used to be quite the thorn in your brother's side, you know.
Don't think he beat me a single game in the last three years of his life--Hoh!
And that's after his chess tutor from Naples was through with him.
Let's test your mettle, then. I'll give you first move.
As always, I open with a pawn to center.
And so shall I.
Then where from here? Where, indeed. Hmm...
I don't like to play sober, I'll admit. Shall I pour us a drink or two?
But of course, but of course.
Ah, I quite like this opening. And here's my knight.
Hmm. Let me think a moment.
Polonius, why did your son truly cancel his voyage?
Urgh... excuse me. I feel-- it's a little stifling in here, isn't it? Allow me to stand a moment and catch my breath.
Didn't you know I'd hear of his return the minute he stepped foot on the dock? Didn't you think word would carry?
The little conversation he had with that barkeep in town. How angry he seemed. How full of fire.
I don't understand. When did this conversation happen? What barkeep?
Let's drop the pretenses. I know you brought Laertes here to run me out of my own kingdom, or else run me through.
You think to put him on the throne over me. I saw through your move the minute he returned.
My lord, it's so hot in here, my throat is... it's tightening.
Can we not go outside into the fresh air?
No, we can't.
You tried to play me for a fool.
You may think me a doddering, incompetent version of my brother. But allow me to assure you: I am much more.
(I thought I'd saved him. What a fool I am.)
(But if I reveal myself, he'll only kill me, too.)
And unlike him, I'll do whatever vile thing I must in order to keep my country.
What a shame it is, that you should pass away in such an undignified manner.
(T-that vial--Where is it?)
Something amiss, my lord?
No. Nothing at all. Only... you must excuse me, Polonius.
I've just remembered I promised to meet with someone here in a moment.
It's a private meeting.
Ah. I... see. I'll take my leave, then.
Yes, I think that's wise.
Guards! Guards, to me, to me!
My King? What's happened?
